content.title: Explaining the New “No Tax on Tips” Rules Proposed by the IRS
content.text: On September 19, the IRS issued its first proposed rules on the new “no tax on tips” deduction created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB). The proposed rules clarify how the tips deduction will work, though the rules may change between now and when the IRS finalizes them in the coming months. Below, BPC explains some of the key elements of this proposed rule and how it will affect the millions of workers expected to claim the tips deduction when they file their taxes next year. Eligible Occupations Earlier in September, the Treasury Department published a draft list of occupations that “customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024” and would therefore be eligible to claim the tips deduction from 2025 through 2028. (Under OBBB, the tips deduction expires on December 31, 2028.) The proposed rules reaffirm that list of eligible occupations and provide more details on how Treasury and the IRS selected the 68 occupations (and more than 200 example jobs) that are eligible for the tips deduction. The agencies used a combination of confidential tax data from 2023, congressional guidance, caselaw from the Department of Labor, and survey data to establish the list of eligible occupations. The proposed rules also include data on: The share of wage earners in each of the 68 occupations who reported tips in 2023 The share of all reported tips by each of the 68 occupations Tips as a share of overall wages for tipped workers in each of the 68 occupations The data is limited in certain respects; it does not include independent contractors, workers who had multiple jobs, or tip income not reported to the IRS. It also reflects just one year of information. Nonetheless, the data provide insights on the workers who will benefit most from the “no tax on tips” deduction. The searchable, sortable table below lays out the 68 occupations deemed eligible for the deduction by Treasury and the IRS, along with some statistics on who within these occupations claimed tips in 2023. Just 10 occupations make up 65% of reported tips among single-job wage-earners in 2023, with waiters and waitresses leading the way at 34% of all reported tips. Bartenders (10%), gambling dealers (4%), food preparation workers (3%), and barbers and hairdressers (3%) round out the top 5. Eligible Payments Treasury and the IRS offer more details in the proposed rules on what types of payment are eligible for the tips deduction: Eligible: Cash, check, credit card, debit card, gift card, electronic or mobile payments settled in cash, and certain tokens (including casino chips). Ineligible: Event tickets, meals, services, and “other assets that are not exchangeable for a fixed amount in cash (such as most digital assets).” As others have pointed out, the rules would seem to rule out cryptocurrency tips, though some ambiguity remains around stablecoins. Tips via Venmo, PayPal, or another mobile app are eligible under the proposed rule, to the extent they are electronic or mobile payments that are settled in cash. Automatic Gratuities Several members of Congress from Nevada had asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to ensure that automatic gratuities are deemed eligible for the tips deduction. Auto gratuities sometimes apply for large parties; for example, when a restaurant automatically applies a 20% tip to parties of six or more people. The proposed rules make clear that auto gratuities are not eligible for the tips deduction, along with service charges and “other mandatory amounts automatically added to a customer’s bill by the vendor or establishment.” Treasury and the IRS offer some flexibility on this rule; they state that such charges are not qualified tips “unless the customer is expressly provided an option to disregard or modify it without consequence” (emphasis ours). This may allow restaurants to, for example: Have a policy that applies a 20% default gratuity to parties of six or more; and Require the waiter to clearly state that the automatic gratuity is optional. Such a sequence, which makes clear to the customer that they can opt out of or modify the automatic charge, may make the payment sufficiently “voluntary” to be eligible for the tips deduction. Further guidance from Treasury and the IRS may be necessary, though. Clarification for Married Couples The Nevada members had also asked for Treasury to allow up to $50,000 in tips deductions for married couples filing jointly where both workers have tipped income. The lawmakers argued that because Congress did not specify whether the law’s $25,000 maximum applied to a particular filing status, Treasury should allow each worker in a married couple up to $25,000 in tips deductions. Treasury rejects that argument, clarifying that “the total amount of qualified tips that can be deducted on a return per calendar year is $25,000 regardless of filing status” (emphasis ours). This is consistent with many other sections of the Internal Revenue Code, where a statutory maximum applies to all filing statuses even if Congress did not separately list maximums by filing status in the law. The “Specified Service Trade or Business” Exception The law limits certain occupations—and workers for certain types of businesses—from claiming the tips deduction. It uses the “specified service trade or business” (SSTB) exception from the Sec. 199A deduction to prevent certain individuals from claiming “no tax on tips.” The following table illustrates how these restrictions may work in practice: Table 1. How the Service Business (SSTB) Restriction Works in the “No Tax on Tips” SSTB BusinessNon-SSTB BusinessSSTB Worker– Not eligible for tips deduction (W-2 or 1099)– May be eligible for tips deduction if W-2 worker– Not eligible for tips deduction if 1099Non-SSTB Worker– Not eligible for tips deduction if W-2– May be eligible for tips deduction if 1099– Eligible for tips deduction (W-2 or 1099) Treasury and IRS provide several examples in the proposed rules, including: A self-employed (1099) comedian (SSTB worker) performs at a venue and receives tips. The tips are not eligible for the deduction because the comedian falls under SSTB. A bartender (W-2) at a company (non-SSTB) works at a theater (potentially SSTB) that contracts with the company for bartending services and receives tips. The tips are eligible because the company is non-SSTB and the worker is an eligible occupation. Additional guidance from Treasury and the IRS may be necessary, especially since C corporations that have not previously been affected by SSTB rules will have to determine what share of their income or revenue comes from SSTB activities. Eligible Workers Of note, Treasury and the IRS provided their first formal estimate for how many tax returns will report tips in 2026: more than 10 million. This is notably higher than previous estimates of workers in tipped occupations, though it still represents a small portion of overall workers in the U.S. Since the deduction provides an outsized tax benefit—estimated at $32 billion—for a narrow slice of workers, some have questioned how the deduction will change economic behavior. Will workers shift from non-tipped to tipped occupations to shield income from taxation? Will consumers change their tipping habits? These questions remain unanswered. Conclusion While the proposed guidance provides much-needed clarity on key questions—such as eligible occupations, types of payments, and the treatment of automatic gratuities—further refinements will likely emerge through public comments and ongoing dialogue. Until then, workers, employers, and tax practitioners alike will be watching closely to see what changes are made and how remaining ambiguities are resolved.
